newsitem.title: DENMARK: SAS Q1 earnings hit by competition.
newsitem.headline: SAS Q1 earnings hit by competition.

text.p: Scandinavian Airlines System (SAS) said on Tuesday that increasing competition in its home territory plunged it into a 269 million Swedish crown ($34.1 million) pre-tax loss in the first quarter of 1997.
But announcing the figures on Tuesday SAS stuck to an earlier forecast of full-year pre-tax profits on a par with its 1996 result of 1.815 billion crowns profit.

"Higher volume and revenue growth than in the first quarter is expected in the remaining three quarters. Increased traffic will also affect unit costs positively during the rest of the year. Several initiatives to improve results are under way which will improve earning and reduce costs," the report said.
The first quarter loss -- compared to profit of 311 million crowns during the same period last year -- was exacerbated by Easter falling in March rather than April.
"That affects traffic volume, especially business travel," the report said, adding that volume in April 1997 -- which would be reflected in second-quarter figures -- was up 11 percent on April 1996.
It said that the early Easter took approximately 150 million crowns from first quarter profits.
Air travel deregulation had also brought more rivals into the airline's Scandinavian backyard.
"Competitive pressure is significant and there has been a marked buildup in traffic capacity to and from Scandinavia by several European players," the report said.
But it nevertheless said that its passenger traffic was unchanged compared with the same period last year.

Last month Norway's privately-owned Braathens SAFE, Finland's Finnair and domestic Swedish carrier Transwede Airways announced plans to increase co-operation in a move seen as an offensive against SAS domination of the region.
British Airways Express, a franchise operated by Danish airline Sun-Air is flying internal Danish and intra-Scandinavian routes.
Virgin Express started flights between Copenhagen and its Brussels base last autumn and is openly eyeing the lucrative Copenhagen-Oslo-Stockholm triangle.
In Tuesday's report SAS said that first-quarter turnover increased to 8.35 billion crowns. from 8.20 billion, but unit costs -- adjusted for currency fluctuations -- rose by 3.6 percent.
Primary factors in the spending rise were increased staff costs and a rise in the price of fuel, it added.
Analysts said on Monday that SAS economy measures were still insufficient.
They had predicted on average first-quarter profits of 172 million crowns, with the most pessimistic forecaster seeing a profit of 45 million.
The results were published after the Copenhagen Stock Exchange closed and the share was unchanged from Monday's closing 70 Danish crowns.
It closed down two Swedish crowns, at 84.00 crowns in Stockholm and fell 3.50 Norwegian crowns to 68.00 crowns in Oslo.
The company is jointly owned by the governments of Denmark, Norway and Sweden and by private investors. Each of the three countries has a locally-traded constituent SAS company.
--Copenhagen newsroom +45 33969650 ($ = 7.884 Swedish Crowns)
